question: Drug companies use AI to scan millions of molecules and pick the few worth testing in the lab. Why does this matter?
answer: Lab testing is slow and expensive, so narrowing the candidate list saves years
choices: Lab testing is slow and expensive, so narrowing the candidate list saves years
AI invents new molecules that have never existed in nature anywhere
AI replaces the need for human clinical trials before sale to patients
AI guarantees that any drug it picks will work on every patient
context: Designing a new drug means picking, from a vast space of possible molecules, the few worth synthesizing and testing. AI models trained on chemistry data can rank candidates by likely activity and likely side effects. Lab confirmation and clinical trials still happen — the AI just shrinks the starting list. Insilico Medicine and Atomwise are two of several companies in this space.

question: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei and other former OpenAI researchers who left over disagreements about AI safety. It's structured as a 'public benefit corporation' (PBC). What's a public benefit corporation, and what's the recognition skill?
answer: A PBC is a for-profit company with a stated public-benefit mission in its charter — but enforcement of the mission is largely up to the company itself
choices: A PBC is a for-profit company with a stated public-benefit mission in its charter — but enforcement of the mission is largely up to the company itself
A PBC is a 100% nonprofit organization — no profits at all are allowed under any state public benefit corporation laws
A PBC is a government agency — public benefit corporations are part of the executive branch under federal law
A PBC is forbidden from raising venture capital — only individual donations are allowed by federal regulations
context: Anthropic is a Delaware PBC. The structure allows directors to weigh public benefit against shareholder return, but enforcement is mostly internal — there's no government inspector ensuring the public benefit is actually delivered. Patagonia is a PBC; so are Allbirds and Warby Parker. The structure can be genuine and can also be marketing. Anthropic also has a 'Long-Term Benefit Trust' that holds special board-appointment rights, layered on top. Recognition skill: corporate-form labels carry less weight than the actual rules. Read the charter, read the operating agreement, and read the incentives — not the press release.

question: The phrase 'AI safety' often gets confused with 'AI ethics,' but they refer to different communities with different concerns. AI safety (Yudkowsky's lineage) focuses on existential risk — superintelligent AI as humanity-ending threat. AI ethics (Timnit Gebru, others) focuses on present harms — bias, discrimination, surveillance. What's the recognition skill?
answer: Read which term a person uses and what concrete harms they name — the labels often hide which group's framing is operating
choices: Read which term a person uses and what concrete harms they name — the labels often hide which group's framing is operating
Treat them as identical — AI safety and AI ethics are interchangeable terms with no community differences
Ignore both communities — only government regulators have legitimate concerns about AI risks of any kind
Pick the louder side — whichever community has more X posts at any moment is correct about AI risks
context: The two communities have had visible conflicts. The 2020 firing of Timnit Gebru at Google (over an internal paper on LLM harms) marked one flashpoint. AI-safety researchers focused on alignment and superintelligence are often (though not always) more sympathetic to incumbent labs; AI-ethics researchers are often (though not always) more critical of incumbent labs. The framings produce different policy recommendations. Recognition skill: a 'safety' argument that ignores present harms and an 'ethics' argument that ignores capability progress are usually telling you something about the speaker's affiliation more than about the technology.

question: Between 2020 and 2022, major social platforms — Facebook, Twitter, YouTube — labeled, restricted, or removed posts containing 'COVID misinformation.' Some labels were applied to claims later acknowledged as factually defensible (lab-leak origin discussion, infection-acquired immunity, mask-policy debates). What's the recognition skill?
answer: When platforms confidently label contested empirical claims as 'misinformation,' read whose authority is being used to define misinformation — and whether it shifts when facts shift
choices: When platforms confidently label contested empirical claims as 'misinformation,' read whose authority is being used to define misinformation — and whether it shifts when facts shift
Platform 'misinformation' labels are always perfectly accurate — every labeled claim was definitively false at the moment of labeling
Platform 'misinformation' labels have no effect — users completely ignore every warning that any platform displays
Platform 'misinformation' labels are required by federal law — every platform is statutorily obligated to label all health content
context: Specific examples by 2023-2024: the lab-leak origin hypothesis (originally labeled misinformation, later treated as a serious possibility by U.S. intelligence agencies and the Department of Energy assessment); natural-immunity claims; school-closure cost-benefit discussions. The episodes don't prove every labeled claim was correct — but they do show that 'misinformation' as a category often tracked the prevailing official position more than independently verified truth. Recognition skill: confident labels on contested questions warrant skepticism, especially when the labels move with policy needs rather than with new evidence.

question: In April 2022, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security announced a new 'Disinformation Governance Board' to coordinate federal responses to misinformation. The board was quickly nicknamed the 'Ministry of Truth' (after George Orwell's 1984), faced bipartisan backlash, and was paused within three weeks. What's the recognition?
answer: Direct federal infrastructure for arbitrating 'truth' provokes immediate constitutional alarm — pressure tends to route through informal channels instead
choices: Direct federal infrastructure for arbitrating 'truth' provokes immediate constitutional alarm — pressure tends to route through informal channels instead
The Disinformation Governance Board still operates today — it makes every official truth determination in the United States
The Disinformation Governance Board was a hoax — no such proposal was ever made by any federal agency
The Disinformation Governance Board is a state-level program — only California ever considered such an office
context: The DHS Disinformation Governance Board, announced by Secretary Mayorkas in April 2022, would have coordinated DHS responses to disinformation. The Orwell comparison was immediate. Civil-liberties groups across the political spectrum objected. The board was paused within weeks and formally dissolved later that year. Recognition skill: the failure of an overt 'Ministry of Truth' doesn't mean the underlying function disappears — it tends to migrate to less-visible mechanisms (informal agency-platform contacts, third-party 'fact-check' programs, voluntary 'industry coalitions'). Watch where the work goes.

question: China's surveillance infrastructure — facial recognition, social credit pilots, internet monitoring, Xinjiang Uyghur tracking systems — is widely cited as the leading authoritarian-AI model. But Western democracies have also expanded surveillance capabilities. What's the recognition skill?
answer: Focus less on whether the technology exists (it does in many places) and more on the institutional restraints that govern its use
choices: Focus less on whether the technology exists (it does in many places) and more on the institutional restraints that govern its use
Surveillance technology is only used in China, and no Western democracy has any facial recognition capability at all anywhere
All surveillance is identical worldwide, and every country has the same institutional restraints on AI surveillance always
Surveillance is impossible to detect, and citizens have no way of knowing whether any government has the capability today
context: Facial recognition systems exist in many democracies. License-plate readers blanket many U.S. cities. Banking transactions are routinely monitored. The difference between China and (say) the UK isn't primarily the technology — it's the legal and political restraints, the role of independent courts, the freedom of press to report on abuses, and the existence of competitive elections that can punish overreach. Recognition skill: 'they have the same tech as us' isn't the analytical question. 'What stops the tech from being used against ordinary citizens?' is.

question: Across many U.S. cities, automated license-plate readers (ALPRs) from companies like Flock Safety and Motorola log every passing vehicle. The data sits in searchable databases for months or years. Police can search for a specific plate's movement history without a warrant in most jurisdictions. What's the recognition?
answer: Driving patterns reveal where you live, work, worship, and visit — passive plate-reader networks build location histories that would have required warrants a decade ago
choices: Driving patterns reveal where you live, work, worship, and visit — passive plate-reader networks build location histories that would have required warrants a decade ago
License plate readers don't actually log any data — every ALPR system deletes all records within milliseconds
License plate readers are universally banned — no U.S. city has ever installed an automated plate reader system
License plate readers affect only criminals — no innocent driver's plate has ever been logged in any database
context: An ALPR network logs every plate that passes a camera, with timestamp and location. Some cities have hundreds of cameras. The records build a detailed picture of every vehicle's movements — including yours, whether or not you've ever been suspected of anything. Police can query the database for any plate without a warrant in most jurisdictions, because the data was already collected and is now 'just records.' Recognition skill: third-party doctrine and bulk collection together produce a level of routine government access to citizen movements that would have been unthinkable before the technology existed.

question: A large industry of 'data brokers' (LexisNexis, Acxiom, Epsilon, Oracle, and many smaller firms) collects, packages, and sells information about you — buying habits, location patterns, family relationships, health inferences, political donations. Most users have never heard of these companies. What's the recognition?
answer: Detailed profiles of your life exist in commercial databases you never agreed to be in — and are sold to anyone with money, including governments
choices: Detailed profiles of your life exist in commercial databases you never agreed to be in — and are sold to anyone with money, including governments
Data brokers don't actually have any data — they are marketing firms that produce no products of any kind
Data brokers are universally banned — federal law prohibits any U.S. firm from collecting any consumer data ever
Data brokers serve only academic research — no commercial customer has ever purchased any data from any broker
context: Data brokers aggregate from many sources — public records, retail transactions, app permissions, websites, and other brokers. Profiles often include hundreds of attributes. Customers include marketers, insurers, lenders, employers, landlords, political campaigns, and law-enforcement agencies. The U.S. has very little federal regulation in this space; California's CCPA and a few other state laws are partial constraints. Recognition skill: 'privacy policy' on a website is largely about how the website itself uses your data — it says nothing about what the broker ecosystem already knows.

question: Tools like Ollama, LM Studio, and llama.cpp let users download open-weights AI models — Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek — and run them locally on a laptop or desktop. No internet connection. No queries logged. No content policy from a remote company. What's the recognition?
answer: Local inference is a structural countervailing force to closed-API content policy — it removes the lab's ability to shape what the model will produce for you
choices: Local inference is a structural countervailing force to closed-API content policy — it removes the lab's ability to shape what the model will produce for you
Local inference is impossible — no open-weights model can run on any consumer computer without massive datacenters
Local inference is universally illegal — federal law prohibits running any AI model outside a major lab's data center
Local inference produces identical output to closed APIs — open weights have no advantage of any kind over closed APIs
context: A capable open-weights model (8B, 13B, 70B parameters) can run on consumer hardware — a gaming PC, an Apple Silicon Mac, sometimes a high-end laptop. The user has full control: no logging, no remote refusals, no policy update changing behavior overnight. Trade-offs: closed-API frontier models may be better at hardest tasks, and self-hosting requires technical setup. Recognition skill: open-weights AI is the AI equivalent of being able to host your own email server, or print your own books. It's a structural check on platform power.

question: In recent elections worldwide — Slovakia 2023, India 2024, Indonesia 2024, the U.S. 2024 — AI-generated audio and video clips of politicians have been used in campaigns. Some clips were quickly debunked; others spread widely before correction caught up. What's the recognition skill?
answer: The first 24-48 hours after a viral clip are the period when correction is hardest to land — by the time the fact-check publishes, the impression has formed
choices: The first 24-48 hours after a viral clip are the period when correction is hardest to land — by the time the fact-check publishes, the impression has formed
AI-generated political content is impossible — no current system can produce convincing fake clips of any politician
AI-generated political content has no effect on elections — every voter ignores every clip regardless of source
AI-generated political content is detected automatically — every platform removes every fake clip within milliseconds
context: Deepfake political clips share a pattern: they go viral fast, spread through trusted channels (often messaging apps where corrections can't reach), and shape impressions before fact-checks arrive. The Slovakia 2023 case (a fake audio of a candidate discussing election fraud) circulated in the 48 hours before voting when election-day silence rules limited media response. Recognition skill: AI-generated content asymmetrically benefits whoever moves first. Build skepticism toward emotional clips arriving without context, especially close to decisions you have to make.

question: Stability AI released the Stable Diffusion image model with open weights in August 2022. It was trained on the LAION-5B dataset, which had been scraped from the internet — including images by living artists who hadn't consented. Several artists sued. What's the recognition?
answer: The legal and ethical frameworks for AI training data lag the technology — practices common in one year can be ruled infringement years later, with no compensation for the original creators
choices: The legal and ethical frameworks for AI training data lag the technology — practices common in one year can be ruled infringement years later, with no compensation for the original creators
AI training-data law has been settled for decades — every lab has had clear written permission for every image used ever
AI training is universally legal worldwide — no court has ever ruled any training practice infringes any copyright anywhere
AI training affects no living artists — every image in every training set was painted before 1900 in the public domain
context: The 2023 class action against Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt argued that artists' styles and works were copied into the models without consent. Getty Images sued Stability AI separately. The cases will take years to resolve. The broader pattern: the AI labs trained on whatever they could scrape, and the legal questions are being adjudicated after the fact. The original creators — most without resources to litigate — are usually outside the conversations setting the eventual rules. Recognition skill: when a technology grows faster than its legal framework, the resulting rules tend to favor whoever was at the table.

question: Some companies have released AI chatbots specifically aimed at children — homework help, tutoring, even 'AI friend' apps for kids. Standard child-data protections (like COPPA in the U.S.) apply, but enforcement is uneven. What's the recognition?
answer: Children's data and chat content are commercially valuable — and the protections kids receive depend on whether the company chooses to follow rules whose enforcement is patchy
choices: Children's data and chat content are commercially valuable — and the protections kids receive depend on whether the company chooses to follow rules whose enforcement is patchy
Children's chat data is automatically deleted by federal law — no company has any record of any conversation with any child
Children's chat data has no value — no company anywhere collects or stores any information from any child user ever
Children's chat data is fully protected by COPPA — no U.S. company has ever been fined for any child-data violation
context: COPPA (Children's Online Privacy Protection Act) requires verifiable parental consent for collecting personal information from children under 13. Enforcement is mostly through FTC complaints, which means violations are discovered after the fact. Several AI-for-kids services have faced complaints. Recognition skill: assume that 'free service for kids' is collecting more data and protecting it less than the company's public statements suggest. The track record of voluntary compliance with child-data rules across the tech industry is patchy.

question: Some critics argue that 'AI safety,' framed primarily as existential-risk advocacy, ends up serving the largest AI labs' interests. The argument: dramatic future-risk framing supports regulation that incumbents can absorb but smaller competitors cannot. What's the recognition skill?
answer: A position can be sincerely held AND serve specific commercial interests at the same time — both can be true, and noticing the second doesn't disprove the first
choices: A position can be sincerely held AND serve specific commercial interests at the same time — both can be true, and noticing the second doesn't disprove the first
Every existential-risk advocate is in the pay of OpenAI — sincerity is impossible in any AI safety position anywhere
Every commercial-interests argument is correct — sincerity has been proven nonexistent for every AI policy position
Both are false — only one of the two (sincerity or interests) can be true at a time about any AI policy position
context: The argument that AI safety advocacy serves incumbent labs (made by figures including Yann LeCun and Marc Andreessen) doesn't prove every safety advocate is insincere. Many are clearly sincere. The argument is that sincerity and commercial alignment aren't mutually exclusive — and watching which positions get amplified by which institutional players is part of analyzing the public conversation. Recognition skill: sincere belief and structural incentive often align — that's part of how influential ideas survive and spread.

question: AI helps cybersecurity defenders — detecting unusual patterns, scanning code for vulnerabilities, automating routine analysis. It also helps attackers — generating convincing phishing emails, finding bugs in software faster, crafting evasion techniques. What's the recognition?
answer: AI affects offense and defense differently — sometimes the same technique benefits both, but the structural advantage often shifts toward whoever automates first
choices: AI affects offense and defense differently — sometimes the same technique benefits both, but the structural advantage often shifts toward whoever automates first
AI helps only attackers — every defensive AI tool has been proven ineffective against any actual cyberattack
AI helps only defenders — every attack-side AI has been mathematically proven impossible to deploy at any scale
AI affects nothing in cybersecurity — the field has been unchanged by AI tools since the year 2000 onward
context: AI-assisted phishing is detectably better than human-written phishing (better grammar, better personalization). AI-assisted vulnerability scanning helps defenders find bugs before they ship — and helps attackers find bugs to exploit. The balance shifts over time and across specific techniques. The recognition skill: dual-use technology favors whoever invests first and at scale, which is often well-resourced attackers (nation-states, sophisticated criminal groups) — until defenders catch up.

question: Algorithmic and high-frequency trading firms (Citadel, Jane Street, Two Sigma, Renaissance) account for a large share of U.S. stock-market trading volume. Their AI-driven trading happens in microseconds. What's the recognition?
answer: Modern stock markets are dominated by algorithmic decisions on timescales no human can match — retail investors operate in a system not designed around them
choices: Modern stock markets are dominated by algorithmic decisions on timescales no human can match — retail investors operate in a system not designed around them
Modern stock markets are entirely human-driven — no algorithmic trading exists in any major U.S. or global exchange
Modern stock markets are universally banned from using AI — federal law prohibits any algorithm in any financial trading
Modern stock markets are perfectly fair to retail traders — every algorithmic advantage was banned by SEC rule in 2018
context: High-frequency trading firms colocate servers next to exchange computers to shave microseconds off trades, run ML models to predict short-term price moves, and execute trades faster than any human can react. The May 2010 'Flash Crash' (Dow dropped ~1000 points in minutes, recovered same day) was driven by algorithmic interactions. Subsequent market structure changes have added some safeguards but not changed the basic dynamic. Recognition skill: markets are infrastructure shaped by whoever builds and operates them; in U.S. equity markets, that's increasingly algorithmic firms — a structural fact retail investors should know they're operating within.

question: Modern AI models are trained partly with the help of human workers who label data — flagging hate speech, ranking model responses, identifying objects in images. Many of these workers are based in lower-wage countries (Kenya, Philippines, India), often working as contractors for companies like Sama and Scale AI. What's the recognition?
answer: Frontier AI is built partly on outsourced labor — under-compensated workers seeing distressing content to make the models more polite
choices: Frontier AI is built partly on outsourced labor — under-compensated workers seeing distressing content to make the models more polite
Frontier AI is fully automated — no human worker has ever touched any training data for any major model ever
Frontier AI uses only U.S. workers — every data labeler for every model is a full-time U.S. employee with full benefits
Frontier AI training data is generated by other AIs — no human worker has ever been involved in any training pipeline
context: Time magazine reported in January 2023 that OpenAI used Kenyan workers via Sama paid under $2/hour to label graphic content (violence, sexual abuse) so the model could detect and refuse it. Similar arrangements have been documented at other major AI labs. The work is sometimes traumatizing; the pay is low; the workers are usually contractors, not employees. Recognition skill: 'AI' often hides human labor underneath. The polished chatbot you talk to was made polite partly by people in lower-wage countries reading the worst content the internet produces.

question: When an AI system causes harm — a wrongful loan denial, a misdiagnosis, an autonomous-vehicle crash — who's legally liable? Existing tort law was written for human actors. What's the recognition?
answer: Liability for AI harm is legally unsettled — who bears responsibility (developer, deployer, user, no one) varies by jurisdiction and is still being worked out
choices: Liability for AI harm is legally unsettled — who bears responsibility (developer, deployer, user, no one) varies by jurisdiction and is still being worked out
Liability for AI harm is fully settled — every U.S. court applies identical rules with identical outcomes always
Liability for AI harm rests on the AI itself — courts have ruled that models are legal persons in every state always
Liability for AI harm is universally borne by the U.S. government — federal taxpayers cover every AI-caused damage
context: Federal courts and state legislatures are working through novel liability questions. Some cases extend product-liability frameworks to AI; some apply professional-malpractice rules; some find no liability for anyone. The EU AI Act includes specific liability provisions; the U.S. is more fragmented. Recognition skill: 'who pays when AI is wrong' is one of the most consequential legal questions being decided right now, and the answer will shape what AI gets built, deployed, and refused.

question: When a business builds applications on top of a closed-API AI service (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google), the business depends on that lab continuing to operate, not raising prices arbitrarily, and not changing the model's behavior. What's the recognition?
answer: Closed-API dependency creates vendor lock-in — the lab can change terms, raise prices, change the model, or shut down the API, and downstream applications have limited options
choices: Closed-API dependency creates vendor lock-in — the lab can change terms, raise prices, change the model, or shut down the API, and downstream applications have limited options
Closed-API dependency has no business risk — every lab is contractually required to maintain identical service forever
Closed-API dependency is universally banned — federal law prohibits any U.S. business from relying on any AI API
Closed-API dependency guarantees lower costs — every lab is legally required to lower prices each calendar year
context: Vendor lock-in is a classic enterprise software risk; it applies to AI too. A company that built its product on GPT-4 can find itself in a hard spot when OpenAI deprecates the model, raises prices, or changes refusal behavior. Migrating to another lab requires re-engineering. Open-weights alternatives are part of why some companies maintain that option. Recognition skill: 'the API works today' isn't the same as 'the API will work the same way next year' — and the rational hedge is having a fallback you can run yourself.

question: In 2018, investigators identified the Golden State Killer (Joseph James DeAngelo) by uploading crime-scene DNA to GEDmatch, a public genealogy database, and identifying him through partial matches with his distant relatives who had voluntarily submitted samples. What's the recognition?
answer: A person's genetic identifiability depends on relatives' choices — a cousin's submission can reveal everyone in the family tree
choices: A person's genetic identifiability depends on relatives' choices — a cousin's submission can reveal everyone in the family tree
A person's DNA can be hidden from databases by individual choice — every user controls only their own data
A person's DNA is never matchable across relatives — privacy is preserved through second-degree separation
A person's DNA is constitutionally protected — no database can include it under any circumstances
context: Genealogy DNA databases (23andMe, Ancestry, GEDmatch) have become law-enforcement resources. Once a few relatives submit samples, the rest of the family is partially identifiable whether they consented or not. The Golden State Killer case made the technique famous; investigative genetic genealogy has solved hundreds of cold cases since. The recognition skill: genetic privacy is not individually controllable in a world where relatives' choices reveal you. Your aunt's DNA test reveals you, and you had no role in that decision.

question: Eliezer Yudkowsky wrote a March 2023 Time magazine essay calling for an international moratorium on training large AI models — including, in his framing, willingness to enforce the moratorium with military force against rogue data centers if necessary. Yudkowsky's position has been at the apocalyptic end of AI risk advocacy for over two decades. What's the recognition?
answer: The 'shut it all down' position is a real position held by named people with stated reasons — it deserves to be engaged as a position, not dismissed and not endorsed
choices: The 'shut it all down' position is a real position held by named people with stated reasons — it deserves to be engaged as a position, not dismissed and not endorsed
Yudkowsky has never advocated for AI restriction — no Time magazine essay exists
Yudkowsky's position has been formally adopted as US policy — military strikes on data centers are authorized
Yudkowsky's position is universally accepted — no AI researcher disagrees with the moratorium framing
context: Yudkowsky's MIRI (Machine Intelligence Research Institute) has argued for decades that misaligned superintelligence is the dominant existential risk of this century. The 2023 essay is the most explicit version of the policy implication: stop training, by force if necessary. This is a real philosophical position with real proponents and a long history. The bank's stance: name positions honestly, engage their arguments seriously, and let the reader weigh the case. A position can be sincere AND wrong AND influential AND worth knowing about — all at once.

question: In Xinjiang, the Chinese government built one of the most extensive AI surveillance systems in the world: facial-recognition checkpoints, voice-print collection, mandatory biometric DNA sampling, and an Integrated Joint Operations Platform that flags Uyghurs for detention based on behavior patterns like prayer frequency or growing a beard. Estimates suggest a million or more were sent to 're-education' camps from 2017 onward. What's the recognition?
answer: AI surveillance can operationalize ethnic and religious persecution at industrial scale — the system's capabilities scale to whatever the state directs them at
choices: AI surveillance can operationalize ethnic and religious persecution at industrial scale — the system's capabilities scale to whatever the state directs them at
AI surveillance is incompatible with persecution — every system technically requires impartial application across populations
AI surveillance was used only briefly in Xinjiang — the program was dismantled by 2018 according to reporting
AI surveillance has no role in detention decisions — Xinjiang's camps were filled exclusively through informant networks
context: The Xinjiang case has been documented by leaked Chinese government files (the Xinjiang Police Files, the China Cables), satellite imagery, survivor testimony, and reporting by outlets including the BBC, AP, and Buzzfeed. The technical stack includes facial recognition tuned to ethnicity, gait recognition, license-plate readers feeding a central platform, and predictive flagging algorithms. The recognition skill: AI surveillance is a tool; the question is always who points it where. The same technology used for finding criminals can be turned on dissidents, minorities, or anyone the state decides to target — and once the infrastructure is built, the redirection is a policy decision, not a technical one.

question: In 2013, Edward Snowden disclosed documents revealing the NSA's XKEYSCORE program — a system that let analysts search the agency's collected internet traffic by email address, IP, or keyword across petabytes of intercepted communications. The program ran without case-by-case warrants. What's the recognition?
answer: Mass-collection systems quietly invert the warrant requirement — the data is already collected, and an analyst's keystroke decides what to look at
choices: Mass-collection systems quietly invert the warrant requirement — the data is already collected, and an analyst's keystroke decides what to look at
Mass-collection systems require a warrant for every query — each XKEYSCORE search went before a federal judge under the Fourth Amendment
Mass-collection systems were dismantled in 2013 — XKEYSCORE ceased operations the day Snowden published the disclosure documents
Mass-collection systems target only foreign nationals — no US citizen communications were ever searchable through any program of this kind
context: XKEYSCORE was one of the most striking revelations from the Snowden archive: an interface used by NSA analysts (and, via partnership, GCHQ and others) to search internet traffic by simple selectors. The legal framework relied on the FISA Amendments Act Section 702 and Executive Order 12333, neither of which required a warrant for the underlying collection. Reform proposals followed; some passed (USA FREEDOM Act 2015 trimmed phone-metadata bulk collection), most did not. The recognition skill: the question is rarely 'can the government read this?' anymore — it's 'has the government already collected this, and what limits the keystroke that retrieves it?'

question: PRISM, also disclosed in the 2013 Snowden documents, was a program under which the NSA accessed user data directly from major US internet companies including Microsoft, Yahoo, Google, Facebook, YouTube, Skype, AOL, and Apple. The companies' role and the level of cooperation were contested afterward. What's the recognition?
answer: Mass surveillance in democratic states often runs through private companies — the legal regime requires the companies' compliance, and the resulting infrastructure ties the firms to state intelligence work
choices: Mass surveillance in democratic states often runs through private companies — the legal regime requires the companies' compliance, and the resulting infrastructure ties the firms to state intelligence work
Mass surveillance in democratic states cannot involve private companies — federal law prohibits all corporate cooperation with intelligence agencies
Mass surveillance under PRISM was fully voluntary corporate disclosure — no legal compulsion existed at any point
Mass surveillance ended in 2013 — every PRISM-participating company terminated cooperation after the Snowden disclosure
context: The companies' public response in 2013 was a mixture of denial, qualified acknowledgment, and demands for transparency about the legal orders they received. Section 702 of FISA provides the statutory basis; the orders are issued under classified procedures with the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. The recognition skill is structural: when a few large companies hold most of a country's digital communication, intelligence access to that communication runs through them whether they want it to or not. The same infrastructure that makes the services useful makes them surveillance choke-points.

question: In January 2020, Detroit police arrested Robert Williams in front of his wife and two daughters after a facial-recognition system matched him to surveillance footage of a shoplifter. He spent 30 hours in jail before being released — he was the wrong man. Clearview AI and similar firms had scraped billions of social-media photos to build their identification models. What's the recognition?
answer: Facial-recognition errors produce real arrests — and the systems' training data was assembled without the consent of the people in the photos, so anyone whose face is online is in the lineup
choices: Facial-recognition errors produce real arrests — and the systems' training data was assembled without the consent of the people in the photos, so anyone whose face is online is in the lineup
Facial-recognition errors are theoretical — no documented wrongful arrest has resulted from algorithmic misidentification in the US
Facial-recognition systems require consent from photographed people — Clearview AI obtained written permission for every image in its database
Facial-recognition arrests are constitutionally prohibited — federal law bars police from using any algorithmic identification tool
context: Robert Williams's case was the first widely-publicized US wrongful arrest from facial-recognition misidentification; several more have been documented since (Nijeer Parks, Porcha Woodruff). Studies (NIST 2019, MIT Media Lab) found error rates substantially higher for women and people of color. Clearview AI's database — built by scraping public photos from Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and elsewhere — was sold to police departments and private security firms before regulatory action (Illinois settlement 2022, UK ICO order 2022) curbed some uses. Recognition skill: anyone whose photo is online has been entered into surveillance lineups they never opted into.

question: Reporting by +972 Magazine and the Guardian in 2024 described two AI-augmented targeting systems used by the Israeli military in Gaza — 'Lavender,' which identified suspected Hamas operatives from population-scale data, and 'The Gospel,' which generated structure-targeting recommendations. Officials reported very brief human-review windows for each generated target. What's the recognition?
answer: AI targeting systems compress human decision-making — when an algorithm produces targets faster than humans can meaningfully review them, the human-in-the-loop becomes a formality rather than a check
choices: AI targeting systems compress human decision-making — when an algorithm produces targets faster than humans can meaningfully review them, the human-in-the-loop becomes a formality rather than a check
AI targeting systems eliminate civilian casualties — every documented military use has produced zero non-combatant deaths across all conflicts on record
AI targeting systems require multi-hour deliberation per target — no military fields any tool whose human-approval window falls under one full hour of analyst time
AI targeting systems are universally banned under international law — every UN member state has ratified treaties prohibiting algorithmic target generation
context: The +972 and Guardian reporting cited Israeli intelligence sources describing review windows of roughly 20 seconds per name generated by Lavender. Civilian casualty figures from Gaza through 2024 were high by historical urban-warfare standards. The Israeli government disputed elements of the reporting. Whatever one makes of any specific conflict, the structural recognition is broader: once an algorithm can generate targets faster than humans can evaluate them, the practical effect of 'human review' degrades — the human becomes a rubber-stamp rather than a brake. The same dynamic appears in other AI-augmented decision pipelines.

question: The war in Ukraine since 2022 has been called the first 'drone war' at scale. Both sides field large numbers of small drones — some commercially adapted, some purpose-built — with progressively autonomous targeting features. Some systems can now lock onto and pursue targets after losing operator signal. What's the recognition?
answer: Lethal autonomy is arriving in the field faster than international policy debates — the gap between battlefield reality and the diplomatic conversation about it is growing each year
choices: Lethal autonomy is arriving in the field faster than international policy debates — the gap between battlefield reality and the diplomatic conversation about it is growing each year
Lethal autonomy is fully governed by international treaty — every fielded drone requires real-time human approval per shot
Lethal autonomy has been entirely abandoned in Ukraine — no autonomous targeting features are in use by either side
Lethal autonomy is irrelevant to military outcomes — drones have had no measurable effect on the conflict's course
context: Reporting from Ukraine has documented FPV drones with on-board target lock that completes the strike even after the human operator's signal is jammed. International discussions on 'Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems' (LAWS) at the UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons have proceeded for over a decade without binding restrictions. Major military powers have generally opposed broad bans. Recognition skill: the gap between 'what we're using in this conflict' and 'what the diplomatic conversation prohibits' tends to widen during active wars, and the technology that gets fielded becomes a precedent for the next conflict.

question: In November 2020, Microsoft rolled out 'Productivity Score' — a feature in Microsoft 365 that, by default, let administrators see per-employee metrics on document creation, email volume, meeting attendance, and chat activity. After a public backlash, Microsoft removed the individual-employee identification within roughly a week. What's the recognition?
answer: Workplace surveillance defaults can ship quietly inside enterprise software updates — the rollback only happened because the product was visible enough to draw public attention
choices: Workplace surveillance defaults can ship quietly inside enterprise software updates — the rollback only happened because the product was visible enough to draw public attention
Workplace surveillance is constitutionally banned — no employer can monitor employee activity in any form
Workplace surveillance defaults never appear in enterprise software — every product requires opt-in approval from every monitored employee
Workplace surveillance has no impact on employees — knowing they are monitored has been shown to have zero behavioral effects
context: The Productivity Score case was rare because the feature was visible and Microsoft cared about reputational backlash. Most employee-monitoring software (Teramind, Hubstaff, ActivTrak, Time Doctor, Veriato, and many others) operates in less visible ways inside organizations that buy it. Standard features include keystroke logging, screenshot capture, application-usage tracking, and 'productivity' scoring. Recognition skill: by default, software your employer buys to manage you has access to a level of detail about your work that was inconceivable a generation ago — and the configuration choices are made by your employer, not by you.

question: By the mid-2020s, employee-monitoring software (Teramind, Hubstaff, Veriato, ActivTrak, and others) was reportedly used at a majority of large US employers. Features included keystroke logging, screenshot capture, application-usage tracking, idle-time detection, and 'productivity' scoring. Most employees were not told the specifics. What's the recognition?
answer: Continuous monitoring of work activity has become the default in many large organizations — and the monitored employees often have no enforceable right to know exactly what is being recorded
choices: Continuous monitoring of work activity has become the default in many large organizations — and the monitored employees often have no enforceable right to know exactly what is being recorded
Continuous monitoring is universally disclosed — every US employer must provide a detailed list of all collected data points
Continuous monitoring has been banned at the federal level — no US employer has used such software since 2020
Continuous monitoring is restricted to highly classified work — no commercial-sector employee is monitored in any way
context: US workplace privacy law is thin compared with Europe. Notice requirements vary by state (Connecticut, Delaware, New York have notice statutes; many states have none). Employees on company hardware and networks generally have a sharply reduced expectation of privacy under current case law. The monitoring intensified during 2020-2022 remote work and largely persisted afterward. Recognition skill: assume the company-issued laptop, phone, and accounts are monitored at a level you cannot fully audit, and treat them accordingly.

question: The Stanford Internet Observatory (SIO), founded in 2019, became a prominent academic center studying online influence operations and content moderation. House Judiciary Committee investigations and lawsuits (Missouri v. Biden, later Murthy v. Missouri at the Supreme Court) raised questions about coordination between SIO, government agencies, and platforms during the 2020 and 2022 election cycles. Stanford wound down much of the program by 2024. What's the recognition?
answer: The line between academic study of moderation and active participation in it can blur — when researchers coordinate with government and platforms on take-downs, they become part of the moderation system
choices: The line between academic study of moderation and active participation in it can blur — when researchers coordinate with government and platforms on take-downs, they become part of the moderation system
The line between academic study and active moderation is fixed by law — federal regulation requires researchers to be independent observers only
The line between academic study and active moderation has no consequences — coordination has been shown to have zero effect on platform behavior
The line between academic study and active moderation is impossible to cross — every researcher operates entirely independently of any platform or agency
context: The SIO operated programs (the Election Integrity Partnership, Virality Project) that produced reports flagging content for platform review. Court proceedings and congressional reporting in 2022-2024 highlighted that the flagging extended to claims later determined to be true, including discussions of vaccine side effects and natural-immunity research. Stanford announced significant program changes in 2024. The recognition skill: 'research on misinformation' done in close coordination with the government bodies and platforms whose moderation decisions it shapes is a different activity from independent academic study — and the labels can hide the difference.

question: Starting December 2022, journalists Matt Taibbi, Bari Weiss, and others published the 'Twitter Files' — internal documents released after Elon Musk's acquisition of Twitter. The files revealed extensive coordination between Twitter staff, federal agencies (FBI, CISA, others), and outside researchers on content-moderation decisions during 2020-2022. What's the recognition?
answer: Platforms ran systematic moderation pipelines with government coordination — the 'community standards' framing understated how much was actually directed by outside agencies
choices: Platforms ran systematic moderation pipelines with government coordination — the 'community standards' framing understated how much was actually directed by outside agencies
Platforms operated entirely independent moderation — no government agency ever contacted Twitter about any specific content decision through any channel
Platforms ignored all government communication — every flagged item was rejected by Twitter trust-and-safety staff without any outside input
Platforms documented every government request publicly — Twitter's transparency reports historically included the full text of every FBI message
context: The Twitter Files documented FBI requests to suppress specific accounts and stories (including the New York Post's Hunter Biden laptop coverage), CISA's role in 2020 election-integrity flagging, regular meetings between platform trust-and-safety staff and federal agencies, and patterns of asymmetric application of moderation policies. The Supreme Court in Murthy v. Missouri (2024) addressed standing but not the merits of the underlying coordination. The recognition skill: 'platforms making their own decisions' was, in important cases, a description that omitted the substantial role of government communication in shaping those decisions.

question: During 2020-2022, major platforms applied 'misinformation' labels, throttling, or removal to a wide range of COVID-related claims — about vaccine side effects, masking efficacy, the lab-leak hypothesis, school closures, and natural immunity. Subsequent reporting and official statements (including from CDC and Department of Energy officials) acknowledged that many of those labeled claims had factual merit. What's the recognition?
answer: Authority-stamped labels can be applied to claims that later turn out to be defensible or true — 'misinformation' is a policy category whose application reflects the moment more than the truth
choices: Authority-stamped labels can be applied to claims that later turn out to be defensible or true — 'misinformation' is a policy category whose application reflects the moment more than the truth
Authority-stamped labels are always correct — no claim ever flagged as misinformation has been later vindicated by any subsequent reporting or official statement
Authority-stamped labels are removed in real time — platforms reverse every labeling decision within minutes of new evidence from any peer-reviewed source
Authority-stamped labels have no measurable consequences — being flagged has been shown to have zero effect on the reach or visibility of any post
context: Examples have been documented retrospectively: lab-leak as a plausible origin theory (FBI and Department of Energy assessments by 2023), vaccine side-effect discussions (myocarditis acknowledgments and updated CDC guidance), school-closure costs (Brown University, Stanford research). Platforms quietly walked back some specific labels and policies in 2022-2023. The recognition skill is general: in a fast-moving information environment, the cost of suppressing later-vindicated claims is rarely accounted for at the time labels are applied, and the same labeling machinery remains available for the next emergency.

question: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), created in 2018, expanded its scope during 2020-2022 from election-system security toward 'mis-, dis-, and mal-information' monitoring on social platforms. Congressional reporting documented CISA's outreach to platforms about specific posts and accounts. Public scrutiny in 2023-2024 led to reduced visibility of these programs. What's the recognition?
answer: Federal agencies created for one purpose can expand into adjacent territory — a cybersecurity agency that becomes a content-monitoring node is doing something other than what its statute described
choices: Federal agencies created for one purpose can expand into adjacent territory — a cybersecurity agency that becomes a content-monitoring node is doing something other than what its statute described
Federal agencies operate strictly within their original statutes — no agency has ever expanded beyond its founding mandate under any administration
Federal agencies are constitutionally required to monitor social media — CISA's content programs were directly mandated by the Cybersecurity Act
Federal agencies have no measurable influence on platforms — no CISA contact has ever resulted in any moderation action by any major social network
context: CISA's original cybersecurity-of-infrastructure remit is broadly uncontroversial. The expansion toward content monitoring drew bipartisan critique by 2023 — Republicans citing speech concerns, civil libertarians citing First Amendment limits, and academic critics citing scope creep. CISA officials in 2024 publicly disavowed some of the content-monitoring activities. The recognition skill: when an agency's mission expands quietly, oversight tends to lag behind the expansion, and the new programs can take on the durability of the agency's original ones.

question: By the mid-2020s, US federal databases (FBI's Next Generation Identification with over 100 million photos, DHS's IDENT, the State Department's facial-image database from passports and visas) plus state DMV photos held biometric records on a majority of US residents. Most of those photos were entered without specific surveillance consent. What's the recognition?
answer: Mass biometric collection in democratic states has come mostly through administrative aggregation — driver's licenses and passports rather than dedicated surveillance programs — but the resulting databases are surveillance infrastructure
choices: Mass biometric collection in democratic states has come mostly through administrative aggregation — driver's licenses and passports rather than dedicated surveillance programs — but the resulting databases are surveillance infrastructure
Mass biometric collection in democratic states has never occurred under any conditions — every photo in every federal database required explicit individual surveillance consent at intake
Mass biometric collection is unique to authoritarian regimes around the world — no United States federal or state database holds any biometric record on any US resident in any form
Mass biometric collection requires a federal warrant per record under existing US law — every face in every federal database was originally added only through formal judicial process
context: GAO reporting and FOIA disclosures over the past decade have documented the scope. State DMV photo databases are commonly used for facial-recognition queries by federal agencies; the queries don't require resident notice. Reform efforts (proposed federal facial-recognition statutes, state-level limits in Illinois and elsewhere) have moved slowly. Recognition skill: the question 'is there a surveillance database that includes me?' for most US adults has a default 'yes' — the operative question is what controls limit the queries against it.

question: A long-running concern in US privacy circles is that surveillance capabilities deployed in authoritarian states for control (facial recognition, predictive analytics, integrated databases) eventually migrate to democratic states for ordinary law enforcement and administration — with the political constraints around their use being the only durable difference. What's the recognition?
answer: The technologies of authoritarian control are not categorically different from those of democratic states — what differs is the political-legal constraints around their use, which can erode without anyone deciding to erode them
choices: The technologies of authoritarian control are not categorically different from those of democratic states — what differs is the political-legal constraints around their use, which can erode without anyone deciding to erode them
The technologies of authoritarian control are technically distinct — facial recognition in China uses entirely different mathematics from US systems
The technologies of authoritarian control cannot exist in democracies — federal law makes their construction technically impossible
The technologies of authoritarian control are universally banned — no democratic state holds any database comparable to authoritarian ones
context: The recognition is Solzhenitsyn's deep point applied: institutional capability is durable across changes in ideology. Building the same database that China uses for repression — passport photos, license plates, biometric collection — does not make a democracy authoritarian. But it builds the infrastructure that an authoritarian regime would use, if the politics drifted. The political-legal constraints (warrants, due process, oversight, judicial review) are what's load-bearing — and those have to be actively maintained, because they erode under emergency justifications and bureaucratic drift.

question: In September 2021, Frances Haugen — a former Facebook product manager — disclosed thousands of pages of internal Facebook research to the Wall Street Journal and the SEC. The documents showed that the company had internal data on Instagram's effects on teen-girl body image, on the algorithm's preference for divisive content, and on the spread of human-trafficking content on the platform. What's the recognition?
answer: Major platforms can have internal research on their products' harms that contradicts their public statements — disclosure usually requires a whistleblower because keeping the research internal is the norm
choices: Major platforms can have internal research on their products' harms that contradicts their public statements — disclosure usually requires a whistleblower because keeping the research internal is the norm
Major platforms publish all internal research routinely — Facebook released every study Haugen disclosed before her whistleblowing went to the Senate
Major platforms do no internal research at all — Facebook had never studied the effects of any of its products on adolescents under any age category
Major platforms are required to publish all internal research — federal disclosure law mandates public release of every internal product study within a quarter
context: Haugen's testimony to the Senate in October 2021 was notable for bipartisan agreement on the seriousness of the disclosures. The internal documents she released included a 2019 study finding that for many teens, 'we make body image issues worse' on Instagram, and that 'aspects of Instagram exacerbate each other to create a perfect storm.' Meta disputed framing and emphasis but did not deny the research existed. Recognition skill: a company that researches its products carefully and publishes nothing of those findings is making a structural decision about whose interests get protected — and the gap between the research and the public framing is where careful readers can find ground truth.

question: Jonathan Haidt, a social psychologist at NYU, argued in 'The Anxious Generation' (2024) that the smartphone and algorithmic-feed transition around 2010-2012 substantially worsened adolescent mental health, especially for teen girls. Critics, including some psychologists, argued the causal attribution to phones was overstated and that other factors mattered. What's the recognition?
answer: The adolescent mental-health deterioration since around 2012 is well-measured and serious — debate over the precise causal mix shouldn't be allowed to substitute for taking the trend seriously and acting on the strongest hypotheses
choices: The adolescent mental-health deterioration since around 2012 is well-measured and serious — debate over the precise causal mix shouldn't be allowed to substitute for taking the trend seriously and acting on the strongest hypotheses
The adolescent mental-health deterioration since around 2012 was a measurement artifact — survey methodologies changed and the underlying numbers held steady
The adolescent mental-health deterioration since around 2012 is fully explained by climate anxiety — no other cause has any evidence
The adolescent mental-health deterioration since around 2012 has been ruled out as caused by phones — Haidt's argument has been entirely refuted
context: The trends are documented by multiple data sources (CDC YRBS, Pew, time-use studies, hospitalization data, suicide rates). The biggest movements are in teen-girl depression, anxiety, self-harm, and emergency-room visits, with sharp inflection points around 2011-2013. Honest engagement: the measurements are robust; the precise causal mix is contested but the case for a strong phones-and-algorithms contribution is serious. Critics include Candice Odgers and others arguing for caution on individual-level effect sizes. Recognition skill: when measurement is solid and causation is contested, precautionary action plus better research beats both denial and overclaim.

question: Multiple researchers, former employees, and Wall Street Journal investigations have argued that TikTok's 'For You' algorithm is qualitatively more aggressive than other recommendation systems at capturing user attention. Cited features include short-loop watch-time feedback, willingness to push novel content into test audiences, and rapid topic-affinity narrowing. What's the recognition?
answer: Not all recommendation systems are equivalent — TikTok's design is widely treated as the high-water mark of attention optimization, and the design is deliberate rather than accidental
choices: Not all recommendation systems are equivalent — TikTok's design is widely treated as the high-water mark of attention optimization, and the design is deliberate rather than accidental
Not all recommendation systems are equivalent — TikTok is the least aggressive of any major platform's algorithm
Not all recommendation systems are equivalent — TikTok publishes its full algorithm publicly with no proprietary components
Not all recommendation systems are equivalent — TikTok has no algorithm and shows content purely chronologically
context: TikTok's algorithm is not technically mysterious — collaborative filtering, content embeddings, watch-time prediction. What's distinctive is the aggressiveness of the optimization loop and the willingness to push content far beyond a user's known interests to find new attention hooks. WSJ's 'TikTok Algorithm Investigation' (2021) traced how rapidly the system narrows into specific topical loops (including disordered-eating content in tests with simulated teen accounts). Recognition skill: 'the algorithm just shows what you like' significantly understates how much the algorithm is shaping your preferences rather than reflecting them.

question: From 2018-2019, journalists (Kevin Roose, Zeynep Tufekci) argued that YouTube's recommendation system tended to push users toward more extreme political content. Later quantitative research, including work by Hosseinmardi, Nagler, and others around 2021, found the algorithm's role was smaller than the initial reporting suggested — user demand and search behavior accounted for more of the consumption patterns. What's the recognition?
answer: Empirical questions about algorithmic effects can be more nuanced than initial reporting suggests — both 'YouTube radicalized millions' and 'algorithms don't matter' are too simple, and serious work requires holding the complexity
choices: Empirical questions about algorithmic effects can be more nuanced than initial reporting suggests — both 'YouTube radicalized millions' and 'algorithms don't matter' are too simple, and serious work requires holding the complexity
Empirical questions about algorithmic effects have a single answer — every study has concluded the algorithm has zero effect
Empirical questions about algorithmic effects have a single answer — every study has concluded the algorithm fully determines every viewing decision
Empirical questions about algorithmic effects cannot be studied — no academic research exists on the topic
context: Honest treatment: YouTube's algorithm matters, user demand matters, the political content ecosystem outside the platform matters. The 2018-19 case-study coverage made the strong claim; later quantitative work tempered it. Platforms also tuned their algorithms in response to the early reporting (YouTube changed borderline-content recommendation defaults in 2019). The recognition skill is general: be willing to update positions on empirical claims as research accumulates, and resist policy framings that treat the strongest possible version of either side as established truth.

question: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein's 2008 book 'Nudge' introduced 'choice architecture' — the idea that defaults and presentations can be designed to steer people toward outcomes the designer considers good without removing the freedom to choose otherwise. AI lets platforms scale this dramatically across billions of users. What's the recognition?
answer: When a single platform's defaults shape billions of choices, the choice architect becomes a kind of quiet sovereign — the political question is who chose the defaults and what accountability there is when the defaults harm users
choices: When a single platform's defaults shape billions of choices, the choice architect becomes a kind of quiet sovereign — the political question is who chose the defaults and what accountability there is when the defaults harm users
When a single platform's defaults shape billions of choices, the architect has no influence — every user decides independently
When a single platform's defaults shape billions of choices, the architect must be elected — federal law mandates democratic selection of default-setters
When a single platform's defaults shape billions of choices, the choices are random — no architect controls any default on any platform
context: The 'nudge' framing was pitched as 'libertarian paternalism' — preserve freedom but design the choice. At small scale (retirement-plan defaults, organ-donor defaults), the framework can be benign. At platform scale, the same logic puts billions of choices on rails that one set of designers shaped. Recognition skill: the political question is not 'whether nudging happens' — defaults exist whether intended or not — but who controls them and what accountability mechanisms exist when the nudging harms users.

question: Mobile sports-betting apps (DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM, and others) grew explosively after the 2018 Supreme Court decision Murphy v. NCAA struck down the federal sports-betting ban. The apps use AI to personalize push notifications, in-game bet offers, and 'bonus' promotions targeted at lapsing users. What's the recognition?
answer: Sports-betting apps are designed to maximize lifetime value from each user — AI personalization finds the moments and offers most likely to extract another deposit
choices: Sports-betting apps are designed to maximize lifetime value from each user — AI personalization finds the moments and offers most likely to extract another deposit
Sports-betting apps are deliberately designed to discourage betting — every notification is calibrated to reduce play across the user base
Sports-betting apps use no AI personalization — every push notification is sent at random intervals to the entire registered user list
Sports-betting apps operate as charitable organizations — they have no business incentive of any kind to encourage continued play
context: Casino design has decades of behavioral-science research behind it — variable reward schedules, near-miss patterns, comp-based reinforcement, loss-disguised-as-wins. Mobile sports betting brings the same techniques into the user's pocket with AI personalization layered on top. Patterns: deposit-bonus structures that lock the bonus in until additional play, targeted win-back campaigns to lapsed users, in-game bet prompts during emotionally salient moments. Recognition skill: the apps are not neutral interfaces — they are engineered systems for behavior shaping, and their job is to keep money flowing in.

question: 'Dark patterns' is a term coined by UX designer Harry Brignull around 2010 for interface choices that trick users into actions against their interests — hidden cancel buttons, confirmshaming opt-out language, pre-checked subscription boxes. AI lets platforms test and personalize which dark patterns work best on which users. What's the recognition?
answer: Dark patterns are not interface accidents — they are deliberate design choices, and AI personalization makes them sharper by targeting each user's specific susceptibilities
choices: Dark patterns are not interface accidents — they are deliberate design choices, and AI personalization makes them sharper by targeting each user's specific susceptibilities
Dark patterns are random design errors — no company has ever deliberately created one of the documented categories
Dark patterns are universally banned in the US — federal law has eliminated them from every interface since 2010
Dark patterns are constitutionally required — federal regulation mandates confirmshaming language on every opt-out screen
context: Categories include 'roach motel' (easy to enter, hard to leave), 'confirmshaming' (pressure language against opting out — 'No thanks, I prefer overpaying'), 'forced continuity' (free trial that auto-converts), 'sneak into basket' (additional items added without explicit consent). The FTC has brought enforcement actions; the EU has consumer-protection rules that apply. AI lets these be tuned per-user — the specific version you see is selected for what works on you. Recognition skill: assume the interface is designed to bias your decision, and read carefully where money is involved.

question: Health, life, and auto insurance pricing increasingly uses AI models with hundreds of variables — credit score, social-media activity in some pilots, purchase history, telematics data from cars, location. The resulting pricing decisions are often opaque to the customer being priced. What's the recognition?
answer: AI underwriting can produce price differences customers cannot interrogate — opacity makes it hard to challenge pricing decisions or know which behaviors changed your rate
choices: AI underwriting can produce price differences customers cannot interrogate — opacity makes it hard to challenge pricing decisions or know which behaviors changed your rate
AI underwriting is fully transparent — every model is published online with all variables and weights for customer review
AI underwriting is illegal in every state — federal regulation requires human-only pricing in every insurance line
AI underwriting matches human underwriting exactly — every model produces identical prices to the traditional process
context: Insurance pricing has long had complexity; AI accelerates it. State 'rate filings' disclose how rates are set in general terms but may not capture the full granularity of AI-driven personalization. Insurance has a discrimination history (redlining, race-based premiums), and contemporary AI raises new versions of old questions. Some states (Colorado, Connecticut) have begun requiring algorithmic-bias testing in insurance. Recognition skill: when prices are personalized via opaque processes, the consumer loses the ability to comparison-shop the underlying logic and to identify discrimination patterns.

question: Resume-screening and video-interview AI (HireVue and similar platforms) became common in the late 2010s and 2020s. Audit studies from MIT Media Lab and ACLU complaints documented that these systems could reflect biases from training data — disadvantaging certain accents, appearances, or backgrounds. What's the recognition?
answer: AI hiring tools can encode biases from the populations they were trained on — and applicants typically have no way to know they were screened by such a tool, much less why they were rejected
choices: AI hiring tools can encode biases from the populations they were trained on — and applicants typically have no way to know they were screened by such a tool, much less why they were rejected
AI hiring tools are perfectly fair by construction — every commercial system has been certified bias-free by federal auditors before deployment in any state
AI hiring tools are illegal nationwide under US labor law — no US employer has been permitted to use any algorithmic resume screening since 2018
AI hiring tools are required to be fully transparent — every applicant receives a detailed explanation of every rejection decision with full mathematical detail
context: HireVue's video-analysis features (later scaled back after public criticism), Amazon's abandoned resume-screening model (which downgraded resumes containing 'women's' as in 'women's chess club'), and many other cases document the pattern. Some jurisdictions (Illinois AI Video Interview Act, New York City Local Law 144 requiring bias audits) have begun mandating disclosure or audits. Recognition skill: when an AI sits between a person and a job offer, the person loses the ability to understand the criteria being applied — which makes detecting and contesting unfair patterns far harder.

question: Many apps that aren't formally gambling — fitness apps with streak counters, language-learning apps with leagues and gems, shopping apps with spin-the-wheel rewards — borrow casino-style variable reward schedules, social-comparison feedback, and loss-aversion triggers. AI personalizes which triggers fire for which users. What's the recognition?
answer: The behavioral techniques developed in gambling have migrated into ordinary consumer apps — same psychology, lower legal scrutiny, broader reach across age groups
choices: The behavioral techniques developed in gambling have migrated into ordinary consumer apps — same psychology, lower legal scrutiny, broader reach across age groups
The behavioral techniques developed in gambling are confined to casinos — no consumer app uses any reinforcement schedule of any kind
The behavioral techniques developed in gambling have been banned in apps — federal regulation prohibits variable rewards outside licensed casinos
The behavioral techniques developed in gambling have no effect outside casinos — context determines whether the techniques produce any engagement
context: Skinner's variable-ratio reinforcement schedules — the most addictive reward structure in operant-conditioning research — power slot machines and many app interactions. Duolingo's gems, leaderboards, and streak-loss panic borrow the toolkit; so do Instagram's notifications, shopping-app spins, and many fitness trackers. The techniques themselves are not new; the personalization layer (which trigger works on which user) is the AI addition. Recognition skill: an app whose engagement mechanics mirror a casino's is using techniques developed in a heavily regulated industry — without the regulation.

question: Political-ad targeting evolved through the 2010s from broad demographic categories toward 'lookalike' audiences, psychographic profiles, and AI-personalized message variants. The technology lets campaigns deliver different content to different voters — sometimes content that would contradict the campaign's mainstream messaging. What's the recognition?
answer: Hyper-personalized political messaging reduces the public's ability to know what a campaign is actually saying — each voter sees a different version, and the cross-talk that used to expose contradictions is absent
choices: Hyper-personalized political messaging reduces the public's ability to know what a campaign is actually saying — each voter sees a different version, and the cross-talk that used to expose contradictions is absent
Hyper-personalized political messaging is universally identical — every campaign sends the same content to every voter under federal law
Hyper-personalized political messaging has no effect — voters ignore all targeted advertising in election outcomes
Hyper-personalized political messaging is constitutionally prohibited — federal law mandates uniform political messaging to all citizens
context: The general worry, raised by researchers including Eli Pariser ('The Filter Bubble,' 2011) and reinforced through Cambridge Analytica and subsequent coverage, is that political discourse fragments into private channels that the broader public never sees together. Reform proposals (universal ad libraries, ad transparency rules, the EU's Digital Services Act provisions) try to push the messaging back into shared visibility. The recognition skill: democratic accountability assumes that what a campaign says can be observed by everyone — hyper-personalization quietly inverts that assumption.

question: AI-generated deepfake images and voice clones became politically and socially consequential through 2023-2024: a fake robocall imitating Joe Biden in the 2024 New Hampshire primary, AI-generated non-consensual sexual images circulating in schools, and increasingly convincing video fakes of public figures. What's the recognition?
answer: Cheap synthetic media has shifted who can produce convincing fake content — what used to require a studio now requires a phone, and the legal framework is catching up slowly
choices: Cheap synthetic media has shifted who can produce convincing fake content — what used to require a studio now requires a phone, and the legal framework is catching up slowly
Cheap synthetic media is technically impossible — no consumer tool can produce convincing fake video or audio
Cheap synthetic media is fully prohibited — federal law has banned all deepfake creation since 2020
Cheap synthetic media has no real-world impact — no documented case of harm from deepfakes exists anywhere
context: The Biden robocall in January 2024 produced an FCC ruling under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and a $6 million proposed fine against the operator. Non-consensual sexual deepfakes targeting students became a frequent K-12 incident; the TAKE IT DOWN Act and state-level statutes (Virginia, California, others) followed. Voice-clone scams against grandparents and businesses (vishing) have scaled. Recognition skill: the cost of producing convincing fake content has dropped dramatically, while the cost of distinguishing it from real has risen — a stable defensive habit (verify via separate channel) matters more than ever.

question: France hosted the AI Action Summit in February 2025, following the UK's Bletchley Summit (November 2023) and Korea's Seoul Summit (May 2024). The French summit was notable for a shift in tone — emphasizing 'innovation' and economic competitiveness more than the existential-risk framing of earlier summits. The US and UK did not sign one of the summit's main declarations. What's the recognition?
answer: International AI summits trace a visible shift in elite framing — the existential-risk emphasis of 2023 gave way to industrial-competition concerns by 2025, reflecting changes in who held political power
choices: International AI summits trace a visible shift in elite framing — the existential-risk emphasis of 2023 gave way to industrial-competition concerns by 2025, reflecting changes in who held political power
International AI summits have had identical framings throughout the series — every summit emphasized exactly the same priorities in the same terms across years
International AI summits ceased operating after Bletchley in 2023 — the French summit and the Korean summit were both canceled before they could take place
International AI summits produce universally binding outcomes — every declaration has resulted in legally enforceable AI regulation in every signatory country worldwide
context: The Bletchley Declaration (November 2023) centered 'catastrophic' frontier-AI risks. By the Paris summit (February 2025), the French government was emphasizing AI as economic opportunity; JD Vance, as US Vice President, gave a speech rejecting heavy regulation; the US and UK declined to sign the summit's main declaration. The recognition skill is about how political fashions shape framings: the substantive questions about AI capability and risk hadn't changed much in 15 months, but the political language around them shifted substantially — and tracking those shifts is part of reading what's actually going on.

question: AI has gone through several 'Summers' (1956-1974, 1980-1987, late-1990s, 2010s-present) and 'Winters' (1974-1980, 1987-1993).
