Each Summer features confident predictions that this time the technology will change everything within a few years; each Winter features funding pullbacks and chastened revisions. What's the recognition?
answer: AI hype cycles have a real track record — confident short-term predictions in each Summer have repeatedly turned out wrong, even though the underlying technology genuinely did improve over the long run
choices: AI hype cycles have a real track record — confident short-term predictions in each Summer have repeatedly turned out wrong, even though the underlying technology genuinely did improve over the long run
AI hype cycles are a media invention with no basis in reality — no real funding pullback has ever followed a period of confident prediction in the field
AI hype cycles always pay off precisely on schedule — every confident short-term prediction has come true within its stated window across the past five decades
AI hype cycles cancel each other out at the system level — confident predictions have produced zero net technological progress in the field over the past decades
context: Marvin Minsky in 1970 predicted human-level AI within 'three to eight years.' The Lighthill Report in 1973 ended UK AI funding for a decade. Expert systems crashed in the late 1980s. The 'AI Winter' funding collapses are documented. The current AI Summer (deep learning, transformers, foundation models) is real — significant capability gains, deployable systems, Nobel-recognized contributions like AlphaFold. The question is whether the short-term predictions of 2023-2025 will track better than 1970's. Recognition skill: long-run technology improvement and short-run prediction accuracy are different things, and the recurring confidence in confident short-run predictions deserves skepticism even when the underlying progress is real.

question: By the mid-2020s, two distinct communities had formed around AI risk: 'AI safety' (associated with EA, longtermism, MIRI, the existential-risk framing, often funded by EA-affiliated foundations) and 'AI ethics' (associated with academic computer science, fairness/bias research, Timnit Gebru's DAIR institute, focused on present-day harms). The two communities sometimes worked against each other. What's the recognition?
answer: 'AI safety' and 'AI ethics' are not the same field — they differ in funding, focal harms (existential vs current), constituencies, and methods, and treating them as one obscures real disagreement
choices: 'AI safety' and 'AI ethics' are not the same field — they differ in funding, focal harms (existential vs current), constituencies, and methods, and treating them as one obscures real disagreement
'AI safety' and 'AI ethics' are completely identical fields — every researcher in either uses the same methods and worries about precisely the same harms in their work
'AI safety' and 'AI ethics' are both fictional categories — no academic community of any size studies AI harms of any kind in any university worldwide
'AI safety' and 'AI ethics' are universally aligned — every safety researcher works on the same projects as every ethics researcher with no methodological difference
context: The distinction matters in practice. Timnit Gebru's 2020 departure from Google (over a paper on large-language-model harms) marked a public flashpoint between the communities. Funding flows show the split — Open Philanthropy and EA sources fund the existential-risk side; foundations focused on equity and labor fund the present-harm side. The communities use different vocabulary, different journals, and have different policy priorities. Recognition skill: 'AI safety' is a term that does work — narrowing the policy conversation to a particular framing of risk while excluding others — and reading whose definition is being used matters.

question: Two basic approaches to AI regulation have emerged. The EU AI Act takes a 'horizontal' approach — defining categories of AI risk and applying rules across all sectors. The US has mostly drifted toward 'sectoral' — existing financial regulators governing AI in finance, healthcare regulators governing AI in healthcare, civil-rights statutes covering AI hiring. What's the recognition?
answer: Horizontal and sectoral AI regulation produce different distributions of compliance burden, oversight expertise, and regulatory-capture risk — neither is automatically better, and the choice itself is political
choices: Horizontal and sectoral AI regulation produce different distributions of compliance burden, oversight expertise, and regulatory-capture risk — neither is automatically better, and the choice itself is political
Horizontal AI regulation is universally superior to sectoral approaches — the EU model has been formally adopted by every developed country and US state by 2025
Horizontal AI regulation is functionally identical to sectoral regulation — the two approaches produce indistinguishable outcomes across every measurable policy dimension
Horizontal AI regulation has been abandoned worldwide — the EU AI Act was repealed by the European Parliament before it ever entered into legal force
context: Sectoral has the advantage of using regulators who already understand the industry (the FDA knows medical devices; the SEC knows financial markets) and disadvantage of producing inconsistencies and gaps where AI cuts across sectors. Horizontal has the advantage of consistency and disadvantage of demanding generalist regulators who may know less about each domain. The choice is partly substantive and partly political — horizontal favors the regulatory class building its own AI expertise; sectoral favors existing agency power. Recognition skill: regulatory architecture choices are themselves political, and the technical framing can hide what's actually at stake.

question: By the mid-2020s, individual US states had passed dozens of AI-related laws — Colorado's AI Act, Illinois's bias-audit requirements, California's deepfake statutes, New York City Local Law 144, Connecticut's notice statutes. The result was a patchwork that varies sharply across state lines. What's the recognition?
answer: In the absence of federal legislation, state-level patchwork emerges by default — the law that applies to a given AI use can depend more on which state the company or user is in than on the technology itself
choices: In the absence of federal legislation, state-level patchwork emerges by default — the law that applies to a given AI use can depend more on which state the company or user is in than on the technology itself
In the absence of federal legislation, no state has passed any AI rule — the field is entirely unregulated
In the absence of federal legislation, every state has identical laws — patchwork is impossible without a federal statute first
In the absence of federal legislation, federal courts have struck down all state AI rules — only federal regulation is constitutionally permissible
context: Federal preemption of state AI law has not happened; preemption disputes are likely as Congress eventually acts. The current patchwork creates real compliance complexity (an HR-software vendor selling to employers in 50 states faces 50 sets of rules) and creates pressure for federal legislation. Whether that federal legislation should be modeled on the strictest state or written to weaken state protections is a political fight, not a technical one. Recognition skill: 'where' a company operates matters enormously for what law it faces — and the politics of preemption is where the next big regulatory battle plays out.

question: Lawsuits over AI training data multiplied through 2023-2025 — The New York Times v. OpenAI, Getty Images v. Stability AI, multiple author cases against Anthropic, Meta, and OpenAI. The core question is whether training a model on copyrighted text or images constitutes 'fair use' under copyright law. What's the recognition?
answer: The legal status of AI training on copyrighted material is genuinely unsettled — courts are working through novel questions, and the outcomes will shape what kinds of AI models can be built and by whom
choices: The legal status of AI training on copyrighted material is genuinely unsettled — courts are working through novel questions, and the outcomes will shape what kinds of AI models can be built and by whom
The legal status of AI training on copyrighted material is fully settled in favor of training — every court has ruled it permissible fair use
The legal status of AI training on copyrighted material is fully settled against training — every court has ruled it copyright infringement
The legal status of AI training on copyrighted material has never been litigated — no lawsuit on the topic exists
context: Early rulings have gone different ways. The Anthropic books case partially upheld fair use for pirated training data (Bartz v. Anthropic, 2025) but allowed claims over the pirated copies to proceed. The Getty/Stability case in the UK had mixed outcomes. The NYT v. OpenAI case has not produced a final judgment as of late 2025. The economic stakes are high: a ruling against training-as-fair-use would force renegotiation of how models are built and might consolidate the industry around companies that can afford licensing. Recognition skill: copyright law and AI capability are genuinely in tension, and the resolution will partly be technical and partly political.

question: Through the 2020s, senior AI-policy and AI-safety positions in US government were frequently filled by people moving from frontier AI companies, EA-affiliated funders, or AI think tanks — and people moved in the reverse direction too. The pattern is familiar from other industries. What's the recognition?
answer: The revolving door between AI companies and AI policy roles creates structural conflicts that don't depend on individual bad faith — people who recently worked for a company, or expect to soon, naturally see questions partly through that lens
choices: The revolving door between AI companies and AI policy roles creates structural conflicts that don't depend on individual bad faith — people who recently worked for a company, or expect to soon, naturally see questions partly through that lens
The revolving door between AI companies and policy roles is universally banned — federal law prohibits any movement between industry and government in the AI sector
The revolving door between AI companies and policy roles has no real effect — every official acts in pure public interest regardless of prior employment
The revolving door between AI companies and policy roles is unique to AI — no other US industry has any similar pattern
context: This isn't unique to AI. Wall Street, big pharma, defense contracting, energy, and many other industries show the same pattern. The AI case is sharpened by the small number of frontier companies and the narrow expert community that policymakers actually consult. Recognition skill: when evaluating an AI policy proposal, look at who's writing the technical details and where they worked before — and where they expect to work after. The conflicts aren't disqualifying, but they shape the available proposals.

question: Chinese AI labs (Baidu, Alibaba's Qwen team, ByteDance, Tencent, DeepSeek, Zhipu, Moonshot) operate under Chinese law, which since 2017 has required private companies to support state intelligence work when requested. Some Chinese AI work is impressive technically (DeepSeek's open-weight releases drew global attention). What's the recognition?
answer: Chinese AI capability is real and growing, and the legal context the labs operate in is structurally different from Western labs — both facts are worth holding together without conflating them
choices: Chinese AI capability is real and growing, and the legal context the labs operate in is structurally different from Western labs — both facts are worth holding together without conflating them
Chinese AI capability is universally fictional — no Chinese lab has produced any functional model
Chinese AI labs operate identically to Western ones — no legal differences exist between the two regulatory contexts
Chinese AI labs are constitutionally banned from any export — no Chinese model is available anywhere outside the country
context: DeepSeek-R1 (released January 2025) drew attention because its capabilities approached frontier-model performance at a fraction of the apparent compute cost, and the weights were openly released. The 2017 National Intelligence Law and 2021 Data Security Law create explicit cooperation requirements with state agencies. Both facts are true — substantial real capability and structural legal embedding in a one-party state. Recognition skill: assess Chinese AI on its technical merits and the legal context separately, and don't conflate criticism of the political environment with denial of the technology.

question: AI companies cite trade-secret protection to avoid publishing details of training data, model architectures, safety testing protocols, and red-teaming results. The arguments include competitive harm and the risk that disclosure would help adversaries circumvent safety measures. What's the recognition?
answer: Trade-secret claims protect legitimate commercial interests AND shield systems from public scrutiny — both are real, and the regulatory balance has to be argued explicitly rather than assumed away
choices: Trade-secret claims protect legitimate commercial interests AND shield systems from public scrutiny — both are real, and the regulatory balance has to be argued explicitly rather than assumed away
Trade-secret claims are universally rejected by US courts — every AI company is required by federal law to publish full model details including weights and training data
Trade-secret claims are universally upheld in every jurisdiction — no AI company is ever required to disclose anything about its training process or evaluation methods
Trade-secret claims have no effect on policy debate — every AI conversation happens entirely on technical merit without any consideration of intellectual-property positioning
context: Mandated disclosures can shrink the trade-secret zone (the EU AI Act has some, US Section 702 reauthorization debate touched on this for federal AI use, and some courts have refused trade-secret protection for source code used in criminal sentencing). The recognition skill is structural: 'we can't tell you how this works' is sometimes legitimate competitive protection and sometimes a shield against scrutiny — and which one a particular claim is doing requires examining the specific information being withheld and the public interest at stake.

question: Google's 'Project Maven' contract with the Pentagon (2017-2018) applied computer-vision AI to military drone footage for object recognition. After protests by Google employees, the company let the contract lapse. Anduril, Palantir, and a wider defense-tech ecosystem have since taken up that work without similar controversy. What's the recognition?
answer: When one set of firms declines defense AI work, others fill the demand — moral concerns at individual companies don't reduce the underlying procurement, they just change which companies supply it
choices: When one set of firms declines defense AI work, others fill the demand — moral concerns at individual companies don't reduce the underlying procurement, they just change which companies supply it
When one set of firms declines defense AI work, no other firm steps in — military demand for AI evaporates without specific suppliers
When one set of firms declines defense AI work, federal law requires them to continue — Google was legally compelled to honor the Project Maven contract
When one set of firms declines defense AI work, the work is abandoned worldwide — no nation pursues military AI
context: Project Maven became a flashpoint inside Google in 2018; thousands of employees signed a protest letter, several resigned, and Google did not renew. The contract moved to Palantir and others. Anduril (founded 2017) has grown into a major defense-AI contractor. The Pentagon's appetite for AI has only grown. Recognition skill: refusing to do morally fraught work as a company is meaningful for those individuals but is unlikely to reduce the work in aggregate — it shifts the suppliers, who often face less internal resistance.

question: Australia's online-safety regulators have pushed for facial-age-verification rules; Canada's AI and Data Act has been in development since 2022; Brazil passed an AI bill in 2024; India has explored AI advisories. The result is that 'AI policy' is being negotiated across dozens of legal systems simultaneously, with different priorities and assumptions. What's the recognition?
answer: AI regulation is now a multi-jurisdiction puzzle, not a single national-policy question — global services must comply with the strictest applicable rule in each market, partition their offerings, or withdraw
choices: AI regulation is now a multi-jurisdiction puzzle, not a single national-policy question — global services must comply with the strictest applicable rule in each market, partition their offerings, or withdraw
AI regulation is universally identical worldwide under a single international treaty — every jurisdiction has formally adopted exactly the same set of legal rules and compliance requirements
AI regulation only exists in the United States and European Union markets — no other country in the world has any AI law on its statute books as of the mid-2020s period
AI regulation produces zero compliance burden for any global service — every multinational platform operates under a single unified set of rules harmonized worldwide by 2024
context: By the mid-2020s, the most-compliance-relevant AI rules across major jurisdictions included the EU AI Act, US state laws (Colorado, California, NYC), UK Online Safety Act, Canadian C-27 / AIDA, Brazilian AI bill, Korean AI Basic Act, Australian online-safety expansions, Chinese AI rules, and a long tail of others. Multinational services face a layered compliance picture. Recognition skill: 'how is AI being regulated?' is no longer well-asked at a country level — it's a global-architecture question, and the answer at any moment depends on the most-restrictive rule in any market the service operates in.
